results.text:
Niko sees the lifted hand.

For a moment he does nothing. Rain stipples the loading arcade between you, turning the freight floor into a wavering reflection of lamps, boots, and descending steel. He has the look of someone who has already decided which questions he will not answer.

Then he comes as far as the dispatch-box threshold and stops beneath its lintel.

Kessa does not rise from her chair. “This is a Guild-lit room,” she says. “Not a holding pen. He may stand there. He does not enter my conversation unless I ask him to.”

Niko gives her a brief nod, more recognition than apology. His gaze finds yours.

“I don’t have Ora with me,” he says. “I won’t tell you where she is, where she was, or what she kept. Don’t ask.”

He lets that boundary stand before continuing.

“I did see why I thought you ought to know I was here.” He glances over one shoulder into the rain-lit arcade. “A woman in municipal gray spoke to a lift scheduler two bays down. Asked whether an auditor had come out of the memorial hall carrying paper. The scheduler gave her nothing useful. I watched her leave toward the canal stairs.”

The word *municipal* feels oily in this room. It proves no office, no sponsor, no link to Aster or Sol. It proves only that someone was willing to spend an ordinary question on your outline.

“I’m not asking you to follow her,” Niko says. “And I’m not offering you a route to anybody. I’m telling you because people who want a person isolated usually begin by learning which door she used.”

Kessa’s cup clicks softly against its saucer. She has not taken her eyes from you.

“The dead-book waits,” she says. “So does my receipt. Neither becomes less true because the arcade has developed a shadow.”

Niko’s face closes slightly at that, as if he respects the refusal to let fear turn every obligation into an emergency exit. He places an open palm against the doorframe.

“If you sign,” he says, “keep the paper in your own hand until you decide who has earned it. If you don’t, don’t pretend the token has stopped asking.”

Outside, a freight lift begins its slow climb, carrying a cage of sealed containers through the rain-bright shaft. Kessa’s dead-book sheet lies beneath the amber lamp. Beside it, the narrow Wickglass receipt waits blank, a fact not yet bought with the sentence it requires.

Niko remains at the threshold, available for only the kind of conversation he has chosen to permit.

"At the shutter you told Ora: west conduit, two turns, then the lift cage. Lose the lane cameras in the condensers." I keep my voice low. "Did that route hold? I am asking you, not writing an answer for you."

You close Ivo’s fingers around the receiver.

“Speaker,” you say. “Your name first. Then the threat. No private arrangements.”

For a moment, he cannot make his thumb obey him. The call glyph trembles beneath it, a tiny green pulse reflected in the rain gathered along his knuckles.

Then Ivo presses it.

The connection takes too quickly.

Not the long, searching delay of a call climbing through dock relays. A single clean tone, and a woman’s voice enters the lane beneath the machinery’s low thunder.

“Ivo.”

He shuts his eyes.

“Ressa.”

The hooded figure beyond the lamp does not move. But the tagged pouch gives one faint, insectile blink from the dolly.

Ressa Morn’s voice is older than you expected, dry and exacting, with no artificial smoothing left in it. “You have called from a dead channel. That means you are frightened, or you have finally learned enough to become expensive.”

“You sent a lane closure,” Ivo says. “You’re transferring my guarantors.”

A pause. Not long. Long enough to hear the rain ticking through a split in the pipework.

“I froze your guarantor route at sixteen-thirty-two,” Ressa says. “I did not transfer it.”

Ivo looks at you. The hope that crosses his face is so immediate it is almost shameful.

Then Ressa continues.

“Do not mistake that for mercy. You missed three restructurings. I froze it because a transfer request came in carrying my book-signature and a priority phrase I retired nine years ago.” Her voice sharpens. “Who is listening?”

“The people who know Calyx’s name,” you say. “And Ora Pell’s.”

The hooded figure’s altered voice cuts across the speaker before Ivo can answer. “She has already said too much.”

Ressa goes silent.

When she speaks again, the coldness in her voice has acquired an edge of something less manageable. Fear, perhaps. Or anger at discovering a hand inside the ledger she has built her life around.

“Put that voice closer to the receiver.”

The figure laughs once, softly. “No.”

“You are not using my book,” Ressa says. “You are wearing it.”

“Same consequence to the people underneath it.”

Ivo grips the receiver until the casing creaks. “Can you stop the closure?”

“I can hold your guarantors where they are,” Ressa says. “For a while. Not erase them. Not extract them. A hold is a flare: whoever forged my authority will know I challenged it, and they will know this handset is live.”

As if summoned by the sentence, the pouch blinks again. This time the silver filament in the exposed paper catches the light and seems to crawl.

Ressa hears the sound through the speaker. “What was that?”

“A tagged Early Continuity fragment,” you say. “Possibly.”

Ivo turns toward the dolly. “They want Ora back for it.”

The quiet on Ressa’s end becomes absolute.

When she returns, her voice has lost none of its severity, but it is no longer merely the voice of a creditor balancing a book.

“Do not bring Pell to them. And do not let that paper touch any networked reader.”

The hooded figure tilts their head. “You recognize the classification.”

“I recognize a trap designed by people who mistake custody for ownership.”

“Can you verify it?” you ask.

“I can tell you whether its stock and registrar hand are plausible. Not whether the names beneath its wash are true.” A breath crackles through the connection. “But Mara—if you send me an image, you hand whoever tagged it a clean line into my debt lattice. They will have every guarantor I still have the means to protect.”

The figure’s gloved hand opens, almost courteous. “There. Even Ressa understands the arithmetic.”

Ivo stares at the call timer. Five minutes have become four. The rage in him has nowhere clean to go. It has begun, at last, to look like resolve.

“What do I owe for the hold?” he asks.

Ressa does not soften it.

“Your presence at my office before dawn,” she says. “No runner. No proxy. You sign a new accounting in front of me, and you tell me every name you sold to buy time. If you fail to appear, I release the freeze myself and let the book take its lawful course.”

It is not rescue. It is a leash with a deadline, offered because the alternative is a stranger using her hands.

“And if I do?”

“I hold your people until we know whose signature is rotting through my ledger.”

The hooded figure steps back toward the rain-dark beyond the lamp. “Accept it, then. Make yourself a debtor twice over. Or decline, and learn whether your bookkeeper means what she says.”

Ressa hears them withdraw. “Ivo,” she says, and for the first time there is something almost personal beneath the hard professional grain. “Do not let them make your family the receipt for a secret they want buried.”

The line remains open. The pouch waits on the dolly, tagged and possibly genuine. Somewhere west, Ora and Niko are carrying the other half of a divided truth through tunnels that have already been priced.

Ivo looks to you—not asking forgiveness, not yet. Asking what kind of damage he is permitted to choose.

“What do I tell her?” he asks.

The lane-closure clock keeps counting down.

Tell Ivo to accept Ressa’s hold and bind himself to her dawn accounting, buying his guarantors time at the cost of a new debt.

Niko does not ask Ora twice.

He drops the emergency lever with both hands.

The shutter rises hard enough to shake rust from its track. Rain-silvered air knifes into the bay, carrying the iron smell of the canal channels and the far-off sweetness of somebody’s tea stall burning cheap sugar. Beyond the threshold, the service lane lies empty for exactly the length of a held breath.

Then a freight dolly rolls out of the dark.

Not fast. Not trying to strike anyone. Its little wheels tick over the grating with an almost domestic patience. A municipal maintenance lamp has been magnet-clamped to its handle, throwing white light across a sealed waterproof pouch and a narrow strip of paper taped to the dolly’s deck.

**ONE HALF FOR ONE NAME.**

Ora sees the pouch and goes still in a manner more dangerous than fear.

“They found a piece,” she says.

“Maybe,” Ivo says.

“Maybe you shut your mouth.”

Niko is already moving. He catches Ora by the elbow—not rough, but absolute—and takes her sideways, away from the line of the shutter. You catch the chained biscuit tin as she lets it go, its weight thudding into your palm. Old metal. Old locks. A small, stubborn gravity.

“West conduit,” Niko says. “Two turns, then the lift cage. We can lose the lane cameras in the condensers.”

Ora digs her heel in. “The other half is not on me.”

“I know,” he says. “That’s why you have to leave alive enough to know where it is tomorrow.”

A sound comes from the opposite end of the service lane: a door unclenching on its seal.

No footsteps follow it.

That is worse.

Niko pushes the shutter just high enough for the bay to become a mouth, not a firing line. He takes position at its edge, scanning the rain-dark geometry beyond. The cutting bar in Ora’s hand looks suddenly ceremonial beside him—an oath from a slower, more honest kind of violence.

Ivo’s receiver wakes.

A single chime, bright and intimate in the pump-noise.

His face drains. He does not touch it.

The display shows no caller. Only a line of dock-contract code, and beneath it, a sentence in plain text:

**THE BOY’S GUARANTOR HAS MISSED TWO SHIFTS. CALL BACK BEFORE THE LANE CLOSES.**

Ivo folds over the receiver as if he has been struck.

“They’re using Ressa’s book,” he says. “Or she is.”

Another movement at the far end of the lane: the vague silhouette of a person beneath a maintenance hood, stationary behind the dolly’s light. They make no move to enter. They do not need to. The pouch waits in the rain between you, offering a fragment of Calyx’s record in exchange for the person who knows how the fragments were divided.

Ora’s eyes find yours. The anger in them has not diminished. It has become calculation.

“Move me,” she says. “But don’t let them make my route into a rescue story. They are not here for me alone.”

Behind you, the hall’s thick walls keep Elian, Tam, Calyx, Ren, and the newly durable account beyond easy reach. Ahead, the west conduit is narrow, wet, and unmonitored only because it was never meant to carry people. Niko can get Ora moving now—but the dolly, the pouch, and Ivo’s threatened family will remain in the lane for someone else to own.

The figure under the hood lifts one hand and taps the sealed pouch once.

A counteroffer. Or bait.

What do you carry out of this threshold?

Send Niko with Ora while you stay in the bay to confront the hooded figure and learn what half of the receipt they claim to hold.

The woman in gray waits for you to occupy the space she has left open—the useful space, the one where a person with a title decides whose fear is admissible.

You do not take it.

“The statement isn’t mine to order,” you say. Your throat is dry enough that the words scrape on the way out. You turn, not toward Ren’s seal or Calyx’s ready pencil, but toward Elian. “Elian. If it happens here, at this door—what does that look like?”

The brass key shifts once in Elian’s hand. Rain tick-ticks against the high panes. For a moment she studies Tam through the narrow opening, and there is no rescue in her face, no promise that witnessing will make any of this clean.

Then she looks at Tam directly.

“Not what it means,” she says. “Not who they think it serves. You decide what you can say. You decide what stays off the paper. Calyx writes the limits with the words.”

Tam’s breath catches. They look at the unsigned municipal form, then at the two visitors, then at Calyx.

“And nobody takes me anywhere afterward?”

Elian does not glance at Ren before answering. “Nobody takes you anywhere because they call it protection.”

The woman at the door lets out the smallest breath through her nose. “Mr. Rook cannot guarantee—”

“No,” Elian says. “I can’t.” Her gaze stays on Tam. “I can tell you what they are asking you to give up.”

That lands. Tam’s shoulders do not loosen, but they settle into a shape that can bear weight.

Calyx opens her notebook to a clean page. “I can write a narrow account,” she says. “No inference. No question you do not agree to answer. I will mark each silence as withheld by Mr. Oris, not absent.”

You touch Calyx’s sleeve before the pencil can move.

“One boundary first. The relay’s later pages cannot go down as proof.” You keep your voice low, but not secret. “The spine was severed. The first page was directly seen; the chain after it was not certifiable once the breach pulse fired. We do not repair one bad record by pretending we have another.”

Calyx meets your eyes. The disappointment there is quiet, exacting. Then she nods.

“First-page observation only,” she says. “Later material: unavailable for certification. Any account of it, if offered, identified as recollection or context.”

Vela, beside the dead relay cabinet, lowers her eyes. The sentence costs her too.

The second visitor shifts at the rear wall. Their bright clearance seal catches the lantern light. “Then the alleged three copies cannot support a public account,” they say. “Produce the custodians, or withdraw the assertion that relocation would obstruct them.”

There it is: not a threat, not quite. A hand slipped beneath the brittle ice of your lie.

Ivo goes pale in a way that has nothing to do with the rain. Ren’s jaw hardens. The mourners cannot know which part of the statement is being tested, only that the room has gone suddenly, professionally still.

Tam speaks before anyone can answer for them.

“I’ll make one statement,” they say. “At the door. Calyx writes it. You both give your names and the office that told you to come here. Then you can ask for whatever records you think you’re entitled to ask for in front of everyone who heard you ask.”

The gray woman’s eyes rest on Tam with an expression almost tender, which makes it worse.

“You understand that public circulation may make you impossible to protect.”

Tam looks at Elian, then at the wet-ink notebook.

“I understand private circulation already did.”

Calyx sets the pencil point to paper. Elian remains beside the threshold, not speaking for Tam, only making it harder for anyone else to do so. Across the hall, Ren’s hand hovers near his blind-audit wafer, waiting for a name he can put where a name must remain.

The visitors have been offered a record they cannot quietly manage. They have answered by asking your bluff to become flesh.

What do you spend next?

Mara withdraws the bluff before Calyx writes another line. She tells Tam, Elian, Calyx, Ivo, Ren, and the visitors: 'There are no three copies and no three custodians. I invented them to stop this door from closing. I lied to all of you.' She apologizes without asking forgiveness, insists the lie be marked as retracted rather than laundered into the witness record, and accepts whatever trust or leverage it costs. She still requires the visitors to name their issuer because their own authority remains unsupported.

You let the theory remain where you put it: under your name, pinned down by its own cautions.

Then you step away from the paper.

The movement is small. It alters the room anyway. Calyx’s pencil pauses above the margin. Elian watches you without softening; the brass key is still caught in her fist. Tam stands at the open mourning-room door with rain-muted voices and memorial smoke at their back, looking as if they have been waiting for someone to stop making their fear useful.

“This is yours,” you say.

Your mouth is dry enough that the words scrape. You look at Tam, not the gray coats. “Finish it however you need to. I won’t interrupt again.”

Tam searches your face for the hook in it. Finds none—or finds only the effort not to offer one.

They turn to Calyx.

“Write that I saw the notice before it was erased,” they say. Their voice shakes once, then steadies around the shaking. “Write the wording I gave you: *Priority: ash.* Write that it invoked Vale reference 49-Delta. Write that the footer named Early Continuity custodial review and a supervisory acknowledgment, H. Morrow.”

Ren’s expression hardens at the sound of his own reference, but he does not reclaim the account from Tam. He only inclines his head once, as though accepting a charge that has already been entered.

“And write the limits,” Tam continues. “I did not preserve the original log. I cannot authenticate the footer. I do not know who issued the notice. I do not know whether Hale Morrow wrote it, saw it, or was used to make it look official.”

Calyx writes every clause. The pencil’s small, blunt sound fills the silence between the rain.

Tam draws a breath.

“Write that Len Aster and Davin Sol asked for a private statement after I named that process. Write that I asked for witnesses instead. Write that they would not name an issuing office, signatory, or scope when first asked.” Their gaze travels to the two adjuncts. “And write what they say now.”

Aster’s composure has become a thing held together by training and the knowledge that the hall is listening. She turns toward the waiting blind-audit wafer. For a moment, the rain on the panes is louder than anyone.

“We request,” she says at last, “a voluntary private deferral of Mr. Oris’s account pending custodial-risk review.”

Ren does not look down at the wafer. “Authority to compel?”

Aster’s jaw tightens.

Sol speaks before she can. “None.”

The word falls cleanly. It costs them more than a signature would have.

“Office?” Ren asks.

Sol looks at Aster. This time she meets his eyes, and whatever passes between them is not agreement.

“We cannot name one,” Aster says.

“Then that,” Tam says, “goes in too.”

Calyx does not hurry. She writes their names beside the request, beside the absence of authority, beside the office they refuse to own. When she finishes, she slides Tam the pencil rather than the page.

Tam reads their statement from top to bottom. The hall waits with them. At last, they sign—not a surrender, not an oath to endure whatever comes next. Just their name attached to the limits of what they know and the conditions under which they were asked to disappear.

Calyx sands the ink beneath the memorial lanterns.

Elian loosens her fingers from the brass key by degrees. She does not look at you when she says, “That is how it stays theirs.”

Not absolution. A boundary observed too late to erase the earlier harm, but not too late to matter.

Aster reaches for the unsigned private-deferral form on the mourning table, then stops. She cannot take Tam’s account. She cannot compel its revision. But the wet sheet in Calyx’s hands is now a map of a dead corridor, an exposed contractor, and two named people who arrived with borrowed care.

Outside, a freight train groans through the viaduct’s wet ribs. Somewhere beyond the loading arcade, a municipal bell gives one thin chime and cuts off.

Calyx holds Tam’s completed statement above the carbon press. “This can stay one witnessed original,” she says. “Or it can become copies before anyone decides who is easiest to frighten.”

The gray adjuncts remain at the threshold, unable to force the door and unwilling, yet, to leave their names behind without a counterstroke.

What do you put into the world first?

Require Aster and Sol to sign their request for voluntary deferral and their lack of compulsion before they leave the hall.

You cross the hall before anyone can make a procedure out of stopping you.

The mourning-room door is painted the color of old bone. Rain answers the viaduct above it in a thousand small fists. You put your palm against the wood—not opening it, not yet—and raise your voice until the mourners, the lanterns, the people pretending not to listen all have it.

“I already copied the full pediatric registrar corridor,” you say. “Sent it to three independent witnesses. Moving it now only proves obstruction.”

The lie enters the hall cleanly.

Calyx’s eyes find yours at once. She does not betray you. That is not the same as believing you. Elian’s hand leaves the first-page copy, slowly; the brass key hangs at her side like a question with teeth. Ivo looks at you with a brief, sick recognition. He knows the sound of a fact sold before it exists.

Inside the room, silence holds for one heartbeat too long.

Then the latch turns.

A woman in rain-dark municipal gray opens the door only far enough to stand in it. Tam is visible behind her at the small mourning table, rigid in a wooden chair, both hands flat beside an untouched paper form. A second visitor remains by the rear wall, their clearance seal bright against a plain collar.

“Then your copies should be preserved,” the woman says. Her voice has the polished softness of someone accustomed to calling pressure care. “Our concern is Mr. Oris’s exposure. His account has named a deprecated custodial process. He is entitled to revise, limit, or withdraw that account before relocation makes him a target.”

“Whose relocation?” Ren asks.

The woman’s gaze slides to him, calculating the gray seal at his throat and what it has lately cost him.

“Registrar materials are being transferred under emergency continuity protection.”

“By whose authority?”

“Bereavement clearance,” she says. “And a custodial-risk instruction.”

Ren does not move from the front doors. He does not need to. “Bereavement clearance authorizes support in a memorial venue. It does not authorize a private correction under pressure. A custodial-risk instruction requires an issuing office, a signatory, and a scope.”

The second visitor speaks at last. “The scope concerns minor-witness classifications.”

That phrase changes the air.

Tam’s head lifts. Fear is still there, but it has found a shape sharp enough to use. “I was not a minor witness,” they say. “I was a contractor reading a footer I was told had never existed.”

“No one is asserting otherwise,” the woman says.

“You just did,” Tam answers.

Calyx comes to stand at your shoulder, paper and pencil held visibly in both hands. “State your names for the memorial record,” she says. “State the issuing office. State whether this alleged instruction directs removal, revision, or silence.”

The woman looks past Calyx, toward the gathered mourners. Her smile does not reach her eyes.

“You have made this needlessly public.”

“No,” Elian says from the memorial table. Her voice is quiet, and it carries farther than the woman’s. “You came here because you thought private was easier.”

The lie is still standing between you and everyone who heard it, brittle as ice. But it has bought this much: the visitors have placed *minor-witness classifications* beside an emergency transfer, and neither will now say who signed the order.

The woman lowers her hand from the door. Not surrender. A refusal to give you more for free.

“Mr. Oris,” she says, turning inward, “you may still choose a private statement.”

Tam looks at you through the narrow opening. Then at Calyx’s waiting pencil.

“I choose witnesses,” they say.

The visitors have not left. The unsigned form remains on the mourning table. And every person in the hall now knows you claimed copies that may one day be asked to appear.

What do you do?

Mara keeps the bluff standing for one more dangerous beat, but steps back from authority. She asks Elian—not Mara or Ren—to decide whether Tam's statement happens at the open door, explicitly honoring Elian's boundary that Mara may witness, not command. Mara also warns Calyx not to cite the severed relay's later pages as proof: those pages became legally uncertifiable when the breach pulse fired. She asks Elian and Tam to set the terms.

Elian does not try to stop you. She catches your wrist once—not to hold you, only to make sure you meet her eyes.

“Bring him back if you can,” she says.

It is not an order to save the paper over the person, or the person over the paper. She has learned too much tonight about what those false choices cost.

“I’ll keep this account breathing,” Calyx says, already turning toward the hall and its witnesses.

Ren’s gaze follows you to the loading arcade. “My people can—”

“No,” you say.

The word comes quicker than your exhaustion. His officers would turn a search into a jurisdiction. Whatever has happened in the coolant lanes, it has already had enough of those.

Vela points through the rain-curtain beyond the freight lifts. “Lower return channel. Past the condenser stacks. There’s an old shutter with a saint scratched into it.”

Niko’s cadence does not sound again.

You go.

The arcade gives way to maintenance dark: ribbed metal underfoot, pipes sweating warm water overhead, the station’s hidden bloodstream rushing behind thin walls. Rain from the weather lattice has found its way down through every bad seam. It drips from cable trays in slow, bright beads. Your shoes splash through runoff carrying rust, machine oil, and a pale thread of incense from the memorial hall.

At the third turn, you find the saint.

Someone has scratched a small lantern into the shutter and given it a crooked halo.

It is half-closed.

Inside the narrow service bay, Ora Pell sits on an overturned crate beneath a hanging worklight. She is older than the hall’s mourners, wrapped in a dockcoat patched so many times it has become a map of other people’s hands. One palm rests on a biscuit tin chained to the crate beside her.

Niko stands between her and the opening, wet to the shoulders, one hand braced against the shutter’s emergency lever. He is breathing hard but upright.

Across from him is Ivo Senn.

No weapon. No theatrical threat. Just Ivo in a black raincoat, with both hands visible and fear working visibly beneath his calculation. A service terminal on the wall has been torn open; its small screen shivers with static.

For a second, all three of them look at you as though your arrival has changed the terms. It has not. Not yet.

“I found him,” Niko says. “He found Ora first.”

Ora gives a dry, humorless click of her tongue. “Found my outer door. He never found my paper.”

Ivo’s eyes flick to the chained tin, then away too quickly.

“The third receipt is not in there,” he says.

“Then why are you still staring at it?” Ora asks.

The terminal clears.

A municipal seal blooms on its cracked display—not Continuity blue, but the antique ash-gray used in the old registrar systems. Beneath it, a single line types itself out.

**PRIORITY: ASH. SETTLEMENT OFFER REMAINS OPEN.**

Then another.

Ivo stays by the lantern rack, watching the clock as though it might indict him personally. Aster folds and refolds the corner of her addendum until the paper begins to soften at the crease. Sol keeps his hands visible on the back of a chair.

Rain gives the silence its body. It whispers over the high panes, sluices down the viaduct’s iron ribs, and turns the loading arcade beyond the glass into a wavering corridor of lamps and dark freight.

When you finally speak, your voice is smaller than it was from the tabletop.

“Ren. State the time.”

You swallow.

“Just the time. Don’t settle anything for me.”

Ren looks first at you, then at the clock. His hand stays away from the wafer.

“Eighteen twenty-three,” he says. “Ten minutes have passed.”

Nothing follows the sentence. No dawn arrives to collect Ivo. No word comes from the west conduit. Tam’s folder remains shut because Tam has not reopened it. The unknown channel remains what it has been all night: a shape behind careful people, not yet a name.

Then the loading-arcade door opens.

A woman in a Wickglass Transit Guild jacket steps in out of the rain: slate-blue oilcloth, reflective piping dulled by use, one courier’s satchel strapped diagonally over a broad adult frame. Her hair is shaved close at the temples; water glitters on the small brass studs there. She takes in the hall with the swift, trained glance of someone who knows when a delivery has entered a room already carrying too much.

“Marа Vey?”

She waits for no one to nominate you.

When you acknowledge her, she crosses only as far as the memorial table and sets a bronze token on its scarred surface. It is heavy enough to sound like a small bell. One side bears the Wickglass mark: three interlocked transit lines around a rain-drop. The other is blank except for a stamped number and a narrow, unfilled line where a name might be written.

“Kessa Brin,” she says, touching thumb to temple in the old good-faith gesture. “Wickglass courier.”

Her gaze does not drift toward Tam’s folder.

“This is for you. Personally. It isn’t passage, and it isn’t authority over anybody else’s movement.” Her eyes sharpen just enough to make the distinction stick. “The Guild has an outstanding obligation with your name attached. One conversation, in a Guild-lit room, before the night’s last freight rotation. You may decline it. The obligation does not disappear if you do.”

“A conversation about what?” Ren asks.

Kessa turns her head toward him, polite and unyielding. “The token’s holder may ask that. Not the room.”

Then she looks back to you.

“No one sent me to collect a statement,” she adds. “No one bought a route. That is all I was paid to say.”

She leaves the bronze disk between you and the lanternlight. Does not wait for your answer. Does not linger to become a witness or a suspect. The arcade door closes behind her, and through its rain-blurred pane you see her slate-blue jacket recede beneath the freight lamps until the station swallows it.

The token remains on the table.

So does the actual evening.

What do you do with either of them?

I take the bronze token but state that Kessa Brin is not Sister Calyx and Wickglass has no claim on Tam. I hand it to Ressa Morn—absent from the provisional scene—and ask Ressa to carry nothing until dawn. Tam's shelter remains undecided; Ivo's debt remains due.
